title: Time cost at a glance
introHtml:
Techniques differ hugely in how much time they take. Teaching a paragraph to a friend can take an hour; answering one question about the same paragraph takes half a minute. This table puts every technique in the compendium on one scale so you can choose with your eyes open.

The unit. One "recall question" means answering one question about a paragraph from memory and then checking your answer. That takes about 30 seconds, and it is the baseline: 1×. A "paragraph" means one dense paragraph of about 150 words that you have already read once. Every other technique is expressed as a multiple of that 30-second question.

These numbers are rough estimates from typical practice, not measured values. They vary with the subject, the material and how practised you are with the technique. Use them to compare techniques with each other, not as a timetable.

TechniqueTime for one paragraphMultipleValue per minuteUse it for
Flashcard review (one card, once)~10-20 s~0.5×HighDaily upkeep of facts you have already learned
Answering one recall question~30 s1× (baseline)HighChecking and strengthening any key point
Re-reading the paragraph~1 min~2× (low value)LowA quick first pass or a warm-up only
Highlighting~1-1.5 min~2-3× (low value)LowMarking a few spots to turn into questions later
Pretesting (2-3 questions before reading)~1-2 min~2-4×MediumPriming attention before a new chapter or lecture
Blank-page recall of the paragraph~2 min~4×HighSame-day review; finding gaps fast
Spaced repetition over a month (about 5 short reviews)~2-3 min in total, spread out~4-6×HighAnything you must still know in months
Practice question (exam-style, incl. reading the explanation)~2-3 min~4-6×HighApplying knowledge; exam preparation
Successive relearning (recall to criterion now + 3 later sessions)~3-4 min in total, spread out~6-8×HighCore material that must be solid
Making flashcards for the paragraph (2-4 cards)~3-5 min~6-10×MediumFacts you will review many times
Elaborative interrogation (2-3 "why?" questions answered)~3-5 min~6-10×MediumTurning isolated facts into connected knowledge
Self-explanation~3-5 min~6-10×MediumWorked examples, mechanisms, proofs
Concrete examples (find or invent 2)~3-5 min~6-10×MediumAbstract principles
Interleaving~0 extra; it changes the order, not the amount (feels ~20-30% slower)~1×HighProblem types or concepts that are easy to confuse
Cornell / question-based notes+2-4 min over plain notes~4-8×MediumNotes you will later quiz yourself from
Mnemonic / acronym for a list~2-5 min per list~4-10×MediumArbitrary lists with no logic of their own
Chunking / grouping~2-5 min~4-10×MediumLong lists that can be sorted into groups
Dual coding (quick sketch + labels)~5-10 min~10-20×MediumProcesses, structures, timelines
Comparison table~10-20 min per table (covers several paragraphs)~20-40×MediumSimilar items you keep mixing up
Concept map from memory~10-15 min~20-30×MediumSeeing how a whole topic fits together
Feynman write-up (plain explanation)~8-15 min~15-30×Low for details, high for key ideasThe few ideas everything else depends on
Memory palace (set up for a 10-item list)~10-20 min~20-40×Low for most materialOrdered lists you must recall exactly
One-page summary of a topic~15-30 min per topic~30-60×MediumEnd of a topic, choosing what matters
Teaching a friend (incl. preparation)~20-40 min~40-80×Low per minute, high for core ideasConsolidating the central ideas of a topic

"Value per minute" is a rough judgement of how much lasting learning each minute buys for typical material, combining the time cost with the strength of the evidence.

items.title: Retention per minute vs depth
items.leadHtml: Cheap techniques (recall questions, flashcards, practice questions) give the most retention per minute. They should be the daily base of your studying, the way staple foods are the base of a diet. Expensive techniques (teaching, concept maps, summaries, Feynman write-ups) give less retention per minute, but they buy something the cheap ones do not: a connected picture of the topic, the ability to explain, and the ability to handle questions you have never seen. That depth is worth paying for, but only for the 10-20% of ideas that everything else hangs on. Spending 40 minutes making a concept map of a list of vocabulary is waste; spending it on the central mechanism of a course is often the best hour of the week.

items.title: Why teaching costs about 50× a recall question and is still worth it
items.leadHtml: Teaching a paragraph to a friend, including preparing, costs roughly 40-80 recall questions' worth of time. For an ordinary detail that is a poor trade: 50 well-spaced recall questions would fix it in memory many times over. But teaching does three things recall does not. Preparing forces you to organise the idea from the start, find the order in which it makes sense, and anticipate questions. Explaining exposes the exact spot where your understanding stops ("and then it... somehow works"). And the listener's questions push you to connect the idea to things you would not have linked yourself. So choose carefully: teach the key concept of a topic (supply and demand, natural selection, recursion, the cardiac cycle), and use recall and cards for the details that hang from it.

items.title: A sample budget: one hour on a 10-paragraph chapter
items.leadHtml:
This is an illustration based on the estimates above, not a measured result.

A passive hour. Re-read the chapter twice (about 20 minutes), then highlight it (about 15 minutes), then re-read the highlights (about 10 minutes), with the rest spent rewriting a few points neatly. The chapter feels very familiar by the end. Almost all of that time is low-value: you have practised recognising the text, not recalling it, and you have no idea which parts you would fail on a test.

An active hour.

StepTimeWhat it buys
Pretest: 5 questions before reading5 minAttention primed for the answers
Read the chapter once, carefully15 minFirst exposure
Blank-page recall of the whole chapter, then fill gaps from the book in another colour15 minYour gaps, found and fixed
Make 8-10 flashcards for the facts you missed10 minA month of cheap spaced review
3 exam-style practice questions, with explanations7 minApplication and a reality check
Feynman write-up of the one key idea8 minDeep understanding where it counts
Total60 min

The active hour reads the chapter only once, yet it produces about 20 retrieval attempts, a list of known gaps, a set of cards for future reviews, and one idea you can explain in plain words. It also feels harder and less satisfying than the passive hour, which is exactly the trap described in "How learning works": the hour that feels best is not the hour that teaches most.
